items.note: Main Paramāra branch began as a vice-regal house of the Rāṣṭrakūṭas under Upendra; Pratihāra decline gave the Paramāras political control of Mālava.
Siyaka II took the title Mahārājādhirājapati and is called the real founder of the Paramāra kingdom; his kingdom reached Vidisha on the east.

Verse 20 of the Udaypur Praśasti of Udayāditya eulogises Bhoja for beautifying the world with Śiva temples (Kedāreśvara, Rāmeśvara, Somanātha, Sunḍira, Kāla, Anala, Rudra); Ganguly and Trivedi differ on their locations.
Vākpati-Muñja as general, poet and patron; he dug many tanks and built temples.
Bhoja's reign opened a brilliant chapter in Mālava art and architecture; epigraphy testifies his temple-building.
Bhoja's Samarāṅgaṇa Sūtradhāra described as a canonical treatise on architecture.
Udayāditya (c. AD 1070-1093) became Paramāra king after Jayasiṃha's end, recovered the kingdom and defeated Karṇa.
The Udaypur temple praśasti of Udayāditya is composed in a style that speaks of the high literary standard of the age.
Udayāditya's signal achievement was the Nīlakaṇṭheśvara (Udayeśvara) Śiva temple at Udayapura, the city named after him.
Nīlakaṇṭheśvara called the quintessence of the Bhūmija style and the model for later Mālava architects.

claim.value: quintessence of the Paramāra Bhūmija; model for later Mālava builders

items.note: In situ inscription on the temple records the hoisting of the flag by Udayāditya in 1080 AD.
Under Naravarman (c. 1093-1134) the Paramāra kingdom, harassed by the Chandellas, Chahamānas and Caulukyas, moved toward downfall; the Madhukargarh inscription records a Śiva temple.
The impostor Ballāla usurped power at Dhārā and was killed by Kumārapāla's army, bringing Mālava under Caulukya rule.
An inscription at Udaypur (Vidisha District), V.S. 1220, says the place was governed that year by Mahāsādhanika Rājyapāla under Kumārapāla of Anahilapāṭaka.
Paramāra princes moved east to the Bhopal and Hoshangabad region; several eastern Mālava Mahākumāras are named.
Lakṣmīvarman's feudatory fought, probably against Chandella Madanavarman, in the Mahādvādaśaka-maṇḍala (parts of modern Vidisha and Bhopal); the start of this chunk is garbled.
Vidisha stone inscription of V.S. 1216 and the Gyaraspur inscription record temples built, images installed and villages granted for worship.
Arjunavarman (c. 1210-1215) annexed Lāṭa but was defeated and killed by Siṃhaṇa, per the Mamdapur inscription of 1251.
Arjunavarman's grants praise him as scholar, poet and patron; Madana, Āśādhara and Bilhaṇa adorned his court.
Iltutmish advanced into Mālava, destroyed the Mahākāla temple and appointed a governor at Vidisha in 1233; Vidisha and Mandhata inscriptions say Devapāla recaptured Vidisha.
Muslim invasion of Mālava; Allauddin Khalji's general overran Ujjayinī, Mandu, Dhār and Chanderi in 1305.
With the decay of the Paramāras their patronage of arts, religion and literature decreased; temple building suffered and ended.
Bhūmija occurs as a temple style in the Aparājitapṛcchā and Kṣīrārṇava; Kramrisch identifies it with temples in Mālava.
Bhūmija śikhara: central offset carried up as an unbroken latā with caitya tracery, rows of kūṭastambha, and a śukanāsā.
Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra on the circular (vṛtta) plan: intermediate rathas built by parivartanā within the circle, yielding the stellate layout.
Most Bhūmija temples lie in territory once under the Paramāras; the style may be called Paramāra or Mālava.

claim.value: Paramāra / Mālava style, supreme expression under Paramāras

items.note: Bhūmija temples may have had a pañcaratha plan before saptaratha; both occur in the extant Mālava temples.
